entries.86c64a1137d0a89c0287066c6613f6ebc46d7c78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10088"/><div sID="gen17996" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10088"/><hi type="bold">13. folly--</hi>literally, "insipidity," "unsavouriness" (<reference osisRef="Job.6.6">Job 6:6</reference>), not having the salt of godliness (<reference osisRef="Col.4.6">Col 4:6</reference>).<div eID="gen17996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17997" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Baal--</hi>in the name of Baal; in connection with his worship (see <reference osisRef="Jer.2.8">Jr 2:8</reference>).<div eID="gen17997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17998" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">caused ... to err--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.9.16">Is 9:16</reference>). <div eID="gen17998" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce3c2397377e16f20ac5063ee0e977c184cf309a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10089"/><div sID="gen17999" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10089"/>14. "Jerusalem" and Judah were even worse than "Samaria" and the ten tribes; the greater were the privileges of the former, the greater was their guilt. They had the temple in their midst, which the ten tribes had not; yet in the temple itself they practised idolatry.<div eID="gen17999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18000" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strengthen ... hands of evildoers--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.13.22">Eze 13:22</reference>).<div eID="gen18000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18001" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as Sodom--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.32.32">De 32:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.10">Is 1:10</reference>). <div eID="gen18001" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e5f81aaad93fc46ee711ef2dcc658a5ecf69ef1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10090"/><div sID="gen18002" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10090"/><hi type="bold">15. gall--</hi>poison (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.8.14">Jr 8:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.9.15">Jr 9:15</reference>). <div eID="gen18002" type="x-p"/>
entries.74c770fa5bee81423a40045e21b5860d56d54166: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10091"/><div sID="gen18003" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10091"/><hi type="bold">16. make you vain--</hi>They seduce you to vanity, that is, idolatry, which will prove a vain trust to you (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.5">Jr 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.15">2Ki 17:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.8">Jon 2:8</reference>), [Gesenius]. Rather, "they delude you with vain promises of security" (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.17">Jr 23:17</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.62.10">Psa 62:10</reference>) [Maurer].<div eID="gen18003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18004" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of their own heart--</hi>of their own invention (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.21">Jr 23:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.14">Jr 14:14</reference>). <div eID="gen18004" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e62195e622aa2b419469a3fdcf3d8ab825cc51e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10092"/><div sID="gen18005" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10092"/><hi type="bold">17. say still--</hi>Hebrew, "say in saying," that is, say incessantly.<div eID="gen18005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18006" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">peace--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.6.14">Jr 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.10">Eze 13:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.10.2">Zec 10:2</reference>).<div eID="gen18006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18007" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">imagination--</hi>Hebrew, "obstinacy."<div eID="gen18007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no evil--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Mic.3.11">Mi 3:11</reference>). <div eID="gen18008" type="x-p"/>
entries.b8e3660edc67b23387e70701d9466092086bb677: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10093"/><div sID="gen18009" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10093"/>18. A reason is given why the false prophets should not be heeded: They have not stood in the counsels of Jehovah (an image from ministers present in a standing posture at councils of Eastern kings) (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.23.22">Jr 23:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.8">Job 15:8</reference>). The spiritual man alone has the privilege (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.17">Ge 18:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Psa 25:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.3.7">Am 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.15">Joh 15:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.16">1Co 2:16</reference>). <div eID="gen18009" type="x-p"/>
entries.c4d19370575cd27c12bd633a4ed3d81606c5003b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10094"/><div sID="gen18010" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10094"/>19. So far from all prosperity awaiting the people as the false prophets say (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.17">Jr 23:17</reference>), wrath is in store for them.<div eID="gen18010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grievous--</hi>literally, "eddying," whirling itself about, a tornado. In <reference osisRef="Jer.30.23">Jr 30:23</reference>, "continuing" is substituted for "grievous."<div eID="gen18011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18012" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fall grievously--</hi>it shall be hurled on. <div eID="gen18012" type="x-p"/>
entries.d892dee7a62a4c11c7f0e407d31e11527d22c426: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10095"/><div sID="gen18013" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10095"/><hi type="bold">20. in ... latter days--</hi>that is, "the year of their visitation" (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.12">Jr 23:12</reference>). Primarily the meaning is: the Jews will not "consider" now God's warnings (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.29">De 32:29</reference>); but when the prophecies shall be fulfilled in their Babylonish exile, they will consider and see, by bitter experience, their sinful folly. The ultimate scope of the prophecy is: the Jews, in their final dispersion, shall at last "consider" their sin and turn to Messiah "perfectly" (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Ho 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.5">Zec 12:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10-Zech.12.14">10-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.13.35">Lu 13:35</reference>). <div eID="gen18013" type="x-p"/>
entries.f0fc0eb8767c524770e573bb0cb77d3b0c416c62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10096"/><div sID="gen18014" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10096"/><hi type="bold">21. sent ... spoken--</hi>"sent" refers to the primary call: "spoken" to the subsequent charges given to be executed. A call is required, not only external, on the part of men, but also internal from God, that one should undertake a pastor's office [Calvin]. <div eID="gen18014" type="x-p"/>
entries.f28cf6dd83847f9aeda2b3825f1391d19b8ca671: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10097"/><div sID="gen18015" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10097"/><hi type="bold">22. stood in ... counsel--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.23.18">Jr 23:18</reference>).<div eID="gen18015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18016" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they should have turned them from their evil way--</hi>They would have given such counsels to the people as would have turned them from their sins (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.5">Jr 25:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.11">Is 55:11</reference>), and so would have averted punishment. Their not teaching the law in which God's counsel is set forth proves they are not His prophets, though they boast of being so (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.15-Matt.7.20">Mt 7:15-20</reference>). <div eID="gen18016" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e64aa80618a7e8fc3535629a7228e137141b715: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10098"/><div sID="gen18017" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10098"/>23. Let not the false prophets fancy that their devices (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.25">Jr 23:25</reference>) are unknown to Me. Are ye so ignorant as to suppose that I can only see things near Me, namely, things in heaven, and not earthly things as being too remote? <div eID="gen18017" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a5dd7c50fe90bcc59d452d5234f3171bac671c7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10099"/><div sID="gen18018" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10099"/>24. (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.7">Psa 139:7</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.2">Am 9:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.3">3</reference>).<div eID="gen18018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fill heaven and earth--</hi>with My omniscience, providence, power, and essential being (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.27">1Ki 8:27</reference>). <div eID="gen18019" type="x-p"/>
entries.bab56660a1f6df60a80b760f86c1cbda5834d2be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10100"/><div sID="gen18020" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10100"/><hi type="bold">25. dreamed--</hi>I have received a prophetic communication by dream (<reference osisRef="Num.12.6">Nu 12:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.13.1">De 13:1</reference>, &c. <reference osisRef="Joel.2.28">Joe 2:28</reference>). <div eID="gen18020" type="x-p"/>
entries.8db40e0f057e96e64ad2262afbb62221496e888c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10101"/><div sID="gen18021" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10101"/><hi type="bold">26. prophets--</hi>a different Hebrew form from the usual one, "prophesiers." "How long," cries Jeremiah, impatient of their impious audacity, "shall these prophecy-mongers go on prophesying lies?" The answer is given in <reference osisRef="Jer.23.29-Jer.23.34">Jr 23:29-34</reference>. <div eID="gen18021" type="x-p"/>
entries.068692e2c07e13aabde2fd1ee276301e11118f5b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10102"/><div sID="gen18022" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10102"/>27. They "think" to make My people utterly to forget Me. But I will oppose to those dreamers my true prophets.<div eID="gen18022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18023" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fathers ... for Baal--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Judg.3.7">Jud 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.8.33">8:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.8.34">34</reference>). <div eID="gen18023" type="x-p"/>
entries.11cb213d1f84540c42fa97a6fa7c6fdc281e8644: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10103"/><div sID="gen18024" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10103"/>28. God answers the objection which might be stated, "What, then, must we do, when lies are spoken as truths, and prophets oppose prophets?" Do the same as when wheat is mixed with chaff: do not reject the wheat because of the chaff mixed with it, but discriminate between the false and the true revelations. The test is adherence to, or forgetfulness of, Me and My law (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.27">Jr 23:27</reference>).<div eID="gen18024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18025" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that hath a dream--</hi>that pretends to have a divine communication by dream, let him tell it "faithfully," that it may be compared with "my word" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2Co 4:2</reference>). The result will be the former (both the prophets and their fictions) will soon be seen to be chaff; the latter (the true prophets and the word of God in their mouth) wheat (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.4">Psa 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.13.3">Ho 13:3</reference>). <div eID="gen18025" type="x-p"/>
entries.cd212e0f1a0ee5aa89ab469d737958fd5e5aebef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10104"/><div sID="gen18026" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10104"/>29. As the "fire" consumes the "chaff," [Jr 23:28], so "My word" will consume the false prophets (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.12">Mt 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">He 4:12</reference>). "My word" which is "wheat" [Jr 23:28], that is, food to the true prophet and his hearers, is a consuming "fire," and a crushing "hammer" (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.44">Mt 21:44</reference>) to false prophets and their followers (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.16">2Co 2:16</reference>). The Word of the false prophets may be known by its promising men peace in sin. "My word," on the contrary, burns and breaks the hard-hearted (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.9">Jr 20:9</reference>). The "hammer" symbolizes destructive power (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.23">Jr 50:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.2.1">Na 2:1</reference>, Margin). <div eID="gen18026" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7c0efa90450d30cb8a3c1446e8aeef2aa9476a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10105"/><div sID="gen18027" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10105"/><hi type="bold">30. steal my words--</hi>a twofold plagiarism; one steals from the other, and all steal words from Jehovah's true prophets, but misapply them (see <reference osisRef="Jer.28.2">Jr 28:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.1">Joh 10:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.19">Re 22:19</reference>). <div eID="gen18027" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7a683c2e708b5e0ec022a8579a4b03c779113a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10106"/><div sID="gen18028" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10106"/><hi type="bold">31. use--</hi>rather, "take" their tongue: a second class (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.23.30">Jr 23:30</reference>) require, in order to bring forth a revelation, nothing more than their tongues, wherewith they say, He (Jehovah) saith: they bungle in the very formula instead of the usual "Jehovah saith," being only able to say "(He) saith." <div eID="gen18028" type="x-p"/>
entries.2650460b1540e21b2c99cbbe0dd33891f3fedc51: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10107"/><div sID="gen18029" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10107"/>32. Third class: inventors of lies: the climax, and worst of the three.<div eID="gen18029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18030" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lightness--</hi>wanton inventions (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.4">Zep 3:4</reference>).<div eID="gen18030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not profit--</hi>that is, greatly injure. <div eID="gen18031" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fc9298822879901c3ada6e74c9543f89387f1f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10108"/><div sID="gen18032" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10108"/><hi type="bold">33. What is the burden--</hi>play on the double sense of the Hebrew: an oracle and a burden. They scoffingly ask, Has he got any new burden (burdensome oracle: for all his prophecies are disasters) to announce (Mal 1:1)? Jeremiah indignantly repeats their own question, Do you ask, What burden? This, then, it is, "I will forsake you." My word is burdensome in your eyes, and you long to be rid if it. You shall get your wish. There will be no more prophecy: I will forsake you, and that will be a far worse "burden" to you. <div eID="gen18032" type="x-p"/>
entries.fcbfa1c878de11dbbe555549bd3073618cdaa1df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10109"/><div sID="gen18033" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10109"/><hi type="bold">34. The burden--</hi>Whoever shall in mockery call the Lord's word "a burden," shall be visited (Margin) in wrath. <div eID="gen18033" type="x-p"/>
entries.fba6f5f51baa7db42f481aa20087c9fee7137423: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10110"/><div sID="gen18034" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10110"/>35. The result of My judgments shall be, ye shall address the prophet more reverentially hereafter, no longer calling his message a burden, but a divine response or word. "What hath the Lord answered?" <div eID="gen18034" type="x-p"/>
entries.b9c7aa48ad8653f2201a8c0fed897edf928a9b54: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10111"/><div sID="gen18035" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10111"/><hi type="bold">36. every man's word ... his burden--</hi>As they mockingly call all prophecies burdens, as if calamities were the sole subject of prophecy, so it shall prove to them. God will take them at their own word.<div eID="gen18035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">living God--</hi>not lifeless as their dumb idols, ever living so as to be able to punish. <div eID="gen18036" type="x-p"/>
entries.df1cf3f8bf16245668de29d0f685f2b00278d41b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10112"/><div sID="gen18037" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10112"/><hi type="bold">39. I will ... forget you--</hi>just retribution for their forgetting Him (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.6">Ho 4:6</reference>). But God cannot possibly forget His children (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.15">Is 49:15</reference>). Rather for "forget" translate, "I will altogether lift you up (like a 'burden,' alluding to their mocking term for God's messages) and cast you off." God makes their wicked language fall on their own head [Calvin]. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.23.36">Jr 23:36</reference>: "every man's word shall be his burden." <div eID="gen18037" type="x-p"/>
entries.99de660f6992eaa9fcfc8f5f1c8f1acf84ef2a90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10113"/><div sID="gen18038" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10113"/><hi type="bold">40. not be forgotten--</hi>If we translate <reference osisRef="Jer.23.39">Jr 23:39</reference> as English Version, the antithesis is, though I forget you, your shame shall not be forgotten. <chapter eID="Jer.23"/>

entries.c0dddd05a285d9e0aa6a6eff53685ca380ce2e9a: <div eID="gen29880" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29881" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29882" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29882" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29881" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29883" type="x-p"/> Sequel of the discourse which commenced in the preceding chapter. The prophet denounces vengeance against the pastors of Israel who have scattered and destroyed the flock of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.1">Jer 23:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.2">Jer 23:2</reference>. He concludes with gracious promises of deliverance from the Babylonish captivity, and of better times under the Messiah, when the converts to Christianity, who are the true Israel of God, shadowed forth by the old dispensation, shall be delivered, by the glorious light of the Gospel, from worse than Chaldean bondage, from the captivity of sin and death. But this prophecy will not have its fullest accomplishment till that period arrives which is fixed in the Divine counsel for the restoration of Israel and Judah from their various dispersions, of which their deliverance from the Chaldean domination was a type, when Jesus the Christ, the righteous Branch, the Root and Offspring of David, and the only legitimate Heir to the throne, shall take unto himself his great power, and reign gloriously over the whole house of Jacob, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.3-Jer.23.8">Jer 23:3-8</reference>. At the ninth verse a new discourse commences. Jeremiah expresses his horror at the great wickedness of the priests and prophets of Judah, and declares that the Divine vengeance is hanging over them. He exhorts the people not to listen to their false promises, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.9-Jer.23.22">Jer 23:9-22</reference>; and predicts the utter ruin that shall fall upon all pretenders to inspiration, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.23-Jer.23.32">Jer 23:23-32</reference>, as well as upon all scoffers at true prophecy, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.33-Jer.23.40">Jer 23:33-40</reference>. <div eID="gen29883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29884" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen29884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29885" type="x-p"/> Wo be unto the pastors - There shall a curse fall on the kings, princes, priests, and prophets; who, by their vicious conduct and example, have brought desolation upon the people.
entries.f07efaa6d0b346b09c664e407af43a37e728dcec: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen29885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29886" type="x-p"/> Ye have scattered my flock - The bad government both in Church and State was a principal cause of the people's profligacy.
entries.31aa87f58d519e577c2698fd0bd37a0bdcd4b8d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen29886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29887" type="x-p"/> I will raise unto David a righteous Branch - As there has been no age, from the Babylonish captivity to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, in which such a state of prosperity existed, and no king or governor who could answer at all to the character here given, the passage has been understood to refer to our blessed Lord, Jesus Christ, who was a branch out of the stem of Jesse; a righteous king; by the power of his Spirit and influence of his religion reigning, prospering, and executing judgment and justice in the earth.
entries.4e829481d32029182180157d491b17be4904ea42: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen29887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29888" type="x-p"/> In his days Judah shall be saved - The real Jew is not one who has his circumcision in the flesh, but in the spirit. The real Israel are true believers in Christ Jesus; and the genuine Jerusalem is the Church of the first-born, and made free, with all her children, from the bondage of sin, Satan, death, and hell. All these exist only in the days of the Messiah. All that went before were the types or significators of these glorious Gospel excellencies. <div eID="gen29888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29889" type="x-p"/> And this is his name whereby he shall be called The Lord Our Righteousness - I shall give the Hebrew text of this important passage: וזה שמו אשר יקראו יהוה צדקנו vezeh shemo asher yikreo Yehovah tsidkenu, which the Septuagint translate as follows, Και τουτο το ονομα αυτον ὁ καλεσει αυτον Κυριος, Ιωσεδεκ, "And this is his name which the Lord shall call him Josedek." Dahler translates the text thus: - <div eID="gen29889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29890" type="x-p"/> Et voici le nom dont on l'appellera: <div eID="gen29890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29891" type="x-p"/> L'Eternel, Auteur de notre felicite. "And this is the name by which he shall be called; <div eID="gen29891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29892" type="x-p"/> The Lord, the Author of our happiness." <div eID="gen29892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29893" type="x-p"/> Dr. Blayney seems to follow the Septuagint; he translates thus, "And this is the name by which Jehovah shall call him, Our Righteousness." <div eID="gen29893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29894" type="x-p"/> In my old MS. Bible, the first English translation ever made, it is thus: - <div eID="gen29894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29895" type="x-p"/> And this is the name that thei schul clepen him: oure rigtwise Lord. <div eID="gen29895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29896" type="x-p"/> Coverdale's, the first complete English translation of the Scriptures ever printed, (1535), has given it thus: - <div eID="gen29896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29897" type="x-p"/> And this is the name that they shall call him: even the Lorde oure rightuous Maker. <div eID="gen29897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29898" type="x-p"/> Matthews (1549) and Becke (1549) follow Coverdale literally; but our present translation of the clause is borrowed from Cardmarden, (Rouen, 1566), "Even the Lord our righteousness." <div eID="gen29898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29899" type="x-p"/> Dr. Blayney thus accounts for his translation: - "Literally, according to the Hebrew idiom, 'And this is his name by which Jehovah shall call, Our Righteousness;' a phrase exactly the same as, 'And Jehovah shall call him so;' which implies that God would make him such as he called him, that is, our Righteousness, or the author and means of our salvation and acceptance. So that by the same metonymy Christ is said to 'have been made of God unto us wisdom, and righteousness and sanctification, and redemption,' <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1Cor 1:30</reference>. "I doubt not that some persons will be offended with me for depriving them, by this translation, of a favourite argument for proving the Divinity of our Savior from the Old Testament. But I cannot help it; I have done it with no ill design, but purely because I think, and am morally sure, that the text, as it stands, will not properly admit of any other construction. The Septuagint have so translated before me, in an age when there could not possibly be any bias or prejudice either for or against the fore-mentioned doctrine, a doctrine which draws its decisive proofs from the New Testament only." <div eID="gen29899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29900" type="x-p"/> Dahler paraphrases, - "This Prince shall be surnamed by his people, 'The Lord, the author of our happiness.' The people shall feel themselves happy under him; and shall express their gratitude to him." <div eID="gen29900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29901" type="x-p"/> I am satisfied that both the translation from Cardmarden downwards, and the meaning put on these words, are incorrect. I prefer the translation of Blayney to all others; and that it speaks any thing about the imputed righteousness of Christ, cannot possibly be proved by any man who understands the original text. As to those who put the sense of their creed upon the words, they must be content to stand out of the list of Hebrew critics. I believe Jesus to be Jehovah; but I doubt much whether this text calls him so. No doctrine so vitally important should be rested on an interpretation so dubious and unsupported by the text. That all our righteousness, holiness, and goodness, as well as the whole of our salvation, come by Him, from Him, and through Him, is fully evident from the Scriptures; but this is not one of the passages that support this most important truth. See on Jeremiah 33 (note).
entries.391e5d89637eb2e31209d3aa34d81471ef0fb369: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen29901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29902" type="x-p"/> The Lord liveth which brought up - See on <reference osisRef="Jer.16.14">Jer 16:14</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Jer.16.15">Jer 16:15</reference> (note).
entries.3de9d11b143e78b9f4b03a7feb357dcf40969c09: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen29902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29903" type="x-p"/> Mine heart within me is broken because of the prophets - The first word of this clause is לנבאים lannebiim, which we incorporate with the whole clause, and translate, "Because of the prophets." But as a new prophecy begins here, it is evident that the word is the title to this prophecy; and is thus distinguished both by Blayney and Dahler, Concerning The Prophets. This discourse was delivered probably in the reign of Jehoiakim. <div eID="gen29903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29904" type="x-p"/> All my bones shake - He was terrified even by his own message, and shocked at the profanity of the false prophets.
entries.4d025dcea0085336fac23661e8ed9c645c59aa8d: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen29904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29905" type="x-p"/> The land is full of adulterers - Of idolaters. Of persons who break their faith to ME, as an impure wife does to her husband. <div eID="gen29905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29906" type="x-p"/> The pleasant places of the wilderness are dried up - He speaks here, most probably, in reference to dearth. Profane oaths, false swearing, evil courses, violence, etc., had provoked God to send this among other judgments; see <reference osisRef="Jer.23.19">Jer 23:19</reference>.
entries.dfff7c17d29db7c8b83fea7519cf0c345113e999: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen29906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29907" type="x-p"/> In my house - They had even introduced idolatry into the Temple of God!
entries.735878466976370bea7ccf15b92c3fdcd784f159: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen29907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29908" type="x-p"/> I have seen folly in the prophets of Samaria - This was not to be wondered at, for their religion was a system of corruption.
entries.7f231360f160c78a41ce8cc2a0a27ed6e91fb1c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen29908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29909" type="x-p"/> I have seen also in the prophets of Jerusalem - That is, the prophets of Jerusalem, while professing a pure faith, have followed the ways, and become as corrupt as the prophets of Samaria. <div eID="gen29909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29910" type="x-p"/> They are all of them unto me as Sodom - Incorrigible, brutish sinners, who will as surely be destroyed as Sodom and Gomorrah were.
entries.dd77afb3fe427edeadb3a64e653ca4501d113751: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen29910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29911" type="x-p"/> Hearken not unto the words of the prophets - That is, of those who promise you safety, without requiring you to forsake your sins and turn unto the Lord; see <reference osisRef="Jer.23.17">Jer 23:17</reference>.
entries.9fe49e34f696f79f268378ea4b7364b29755f15b: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen29911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29912" type="x-p"/> Who hath stood in the counsel of the Lord - Who of them has ever received a word of prophecy from me? My word is not in them.
entries.0747af74a83692297de0c406d4522e8e7b6af44b: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen29912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29913" type="x-p"/> Behold, a whirlwind - The simoom: the hot pestilential wind blowing from the south, frequently mentioned or referred to in the sacred writings; see <reference osisRef="Jer.23.10">Jer 23:10</reference>.
entries.c02c536260b19cc11678d8f00eca31a103b23f1c: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen29913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29914" type="x-p"/> In the latter days ye shall consider it - I give you warning: and this punishment which I now threaten shall surely take place; a short time will determine it; ye shall not escape.
entries.564b1b735486547aeb96bc8592af0bed1756b3d8: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen29914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29915" type="x-p"/> I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran - Not to save souls, but to profit themselves. <div eID="gen29915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29916" type="x-p"/> I have not spoken to them, yet they prophesied - They never received the word at my mouth; yet they went, publishing their own deceits, and pretending them to be revelations from God. The churches which have legal emoluments are ever in danger of being overrun and ruined by worldly and self-interested priests.
entries.28f247c4d52f69715c16e39a8ae8c5e479581b33: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen29916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29917" type="x-p"/> Am I a God at hand, - and not a God afar off? - You act as if you thought I could not see you! Am I not omnipresent? Do not I fill the heavens and the earth? <reference osisRef="Jer.23.24">Jer 23:24</reference>.
entries.1569f52bd19e5576932f41b54702688589bd3378: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen29917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29918" type="x-p"/> Bay their dreams - Dreams were anciently reputed as a species of inspiration; see <reference osisRef="Num.12.6">Num 12:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.6">1Sam 28:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joe.3.1">Joe 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.1">Dan 7:1</reference>. In the Book of Genesis we find many examples; and although many mistook the workings of their own vain imaginations in sleep for revelations from God, yet he has often revealed himself in this way: but such dreams were easily distinguished from the others. They were always such as had no connection with the gratification of the flesh; they were such as contained warnings against sin, and excitements to holiness; they were always consecutive - well connected, with a proper beginning and ending; such as possessed the intellect more than the imagination. Of such dreams the Lord says, (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.28">Jer 23:28</reference>): The prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream - permit him to show what he has thus received from the Lord: but let him tell it as a dream, and speak my word faithfully, lest he may have been deceived.
entries.bf43206a82d11fd51efb882ea0b03d4e5ebb29e4: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen29918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29919" type="x-p"/> What is the chaff to the wheat? saith the Lord - Do not mingle these equivocal matters with positive revelations. Do not consider a dream, even from a prophet, as that positive inspiration which my prophets receive when their reason, judgment, and spiritual feelings are all in full and in regular exercise. Mix none of your own devices with my doctrines.
entries.a8d01b0d355212d0b3c6cfa1d10572c2ffa8a31c: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen29919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29920" type="x-p"/> Is not my word like as a fire? - It enlightens, warms, and penetrates every part. When it is communicated to the true prophet, it is like a fire shut up in his bones; he cannot retain it, he must publish it: and when published, it is like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces; it is ever accompanied by a Divine power, that causes both sinner and saint to feel its weight and importance. <div eID="gen29920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29921" type="x-p"/> In the original words there is something singular: הלוא כה דברי כאש halo coh debari kaesh, "Is not thus my word like fire?" I suspect, with Dr. Blayney, that כה coh, thus, was formerly written כח coach, strength or power; and so it was understood by the Targumist: "Are not all my words strong, like fire?" and probably the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews read it thus, and had it in view when he wrote: "For the word of God is quick and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword," <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">Heb 4:12</reference>. This admitted, the text would read, "Is not my word powerful, like fire?" or, "Is not the power of my word like fire?" But however we understand the words, let us take heed lest we think, as some have thought and affirmed, that the sacred writings are quite sufficient of themselves to enlighten, convince, and convert the soul, and that there is no need of the Holy Spirit. Fire itself must be applied by an agent in order to produce its effects; and surely the hammer cannot break the rock in pieces, unless wielded by an able workman. And it is God's Spirit alone that can thus apply it; for we find it frequently read and frequently spoken, without producing any salutary effects. And by this very thing the true preachers of the word of God may be distinguished from the false, non-commissioned ones; those who run, though they are not sent, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.21">Jer 23:21</reference>. The word of him who has his commission from heaven shall be as a fire and as a hammer; sinners shall be convinced and converted to God by it. But the others, though they steal the word from their neighbor - borrow or pilfer a good sermon, yet they do not profit the people at all, because God did not send them, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.32">Jer 23:32</reference>; for the power of God does not in their ministry accompany the word. <div eID="gen29921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29922" type="x-p"/> There may be an allusion to the practice in some mining countries, of roasting stones containing ore, before they are subjected to the hammer, in order to pulverize them. In Cornwall I have seen them roast the tin stones in the fire, before they placed them under the action of the hammers in the stamp mill. The fire separated the arsenic from the ore, and then they were easily reduced to powder by the hammers of the mill; afterwards, washing the mass with water, the grains of tin sank to the bottom, while the lighter parts went off with the water, and thus the metal was procured clean and pure. If this be the allusion, it is very appropriate.
entries.d20ac0cc9133b205cb508fa17b0a399878dc69a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen29922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29923" type="x-p"/> I am against the prophets - Three cases are mentioned here which excited God's disapprobation: <div eID="gen29923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29924" type="x-p"/> 1. The prophets who stole the word from their neighbor; who associated with the true prophets, got some intelligence from them, and then went and published it as a revelation which themselves had received, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.30">Jer 23:30</reference>. <div eID="gen29924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29925" type="x-p"/> 2. The prophets who used their tongues; הלקחים לשונם hallokechim leshonam, who lick or smooth with their tongues - gave their own counsels as Divine revelations, flattering them in their sins, and promising peace, when God had not spoken; and prefaced them, "Thus saith the Lord," <reference osisRef="Jer.23.31">Jer 23:31</reference>. <div eID="gen29925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29926" type="x-p"/> 3. The prophets who made up false stories, which they termed prophecies, revealed to them in dreams; and thus caused the people to err, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.32">Jer 23:32</reference>.
entries.59224ecbe5b94e40f4689d1ced2a806deb741cf4: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen29926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29927" type="x-p"/> What is the burden of the Lord? - The word משא massa, here used, signifies burden, oracle, prophetic discourse; and is used by almost every prophet. But the persons in the text appear to have been mockers. "Where is this burden of the Lord?" - "What is the burden now?" To this insolent question the prophet answers in the following verses. <div eID="gen29927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29928" type="x-p"/> I will ever forsake you - I will punish the prophet, the priest and the people, that speak thus, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.34">Jer 23:34</reference>. Here are burdens.
entries.f0c0746f51ee866d1a506ba880e3eff3e93b2bf2: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen29928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29929" type="x-p"/> Every man's word shall be his burden - Ye say that all God's messages are burdens, and to you they shall be such: whereas, had you used them as you ought, they would have been blessings to you. <div eID="gen29929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29930" type="x-p"/> For ye have perverted the words of the living God - And thus have sinned against your own souls.
entries.22afb0713462796e1b0205d44fbebb045468b18e: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen29930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29931" type="x-p"/> I will utterly forget you, and I will forsake you and the city - Dr. Blayney translates: - I will both take you up altogether, and will cast you off together with the city. Ye are a burden to me: but I will take you up, and then cast you off. I will do with you as a man weary with his burden will do; cast it off his shoulders, and bear it no more.
entries.7d3e6a9160350e4fed9236031b5eab04c16e03aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen29931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29932" type="x-p"/> I will bring an everlasting reproach upon you - And this reproach of having rebelled against so good a God, and rejected so powerful a Savior, follows them to this day through all their dispersions, in every part of the habitable earth. The word of the Lord cannot fail.  <chapter eID="Jer.23"/> <div eID="gen29932" type="x-p"/>

entries.a9267cda22f0be6eff9a2eb96bf3e81c5bcb7ef9: <reference osisRef="Jer.23.1-Jer.23.3">Jer 23:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen14105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14106" type="x-p"/> The gathering again of the flock, scattered by the evil shepherds, by meant of the righteous branch from the stock of David. - Jer 23:1. <hi type="italic">"Woe to shepherds that destroy and scatter the flock of my pasturing! saith Jahveh.</hi> Jer 23:2. <hi type="italic">Therefore thus saith Jahveh, the God of Israel, concerning the shepherds that feed my people: Ye have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and not visited them; behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings, saith Jahveh.</hi> Jer 23:3. <hi type="italic">And I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all lands whither I have driven them, and bring them back to their pasture, that they may be fruitful and increase;</hi> Jer 23:4. <hi type="italic">And will raise up over them shepherds that shall feed them, and they shall fear no more, nor be dismayed, nor be lacking, saith Jahveh.</hi> Jer 23:5. <hi type="italic">Behold, days come, saith Jahveh, that I raise up unto David a righteous branch, that shall reign as king, and deal wisely, and do right and justice in the land.</hi> Jer 23:6. <hi type="italic">In his days Judah shall have welfare, and Israel dwell safely; and this is his name whereby he shall be called: Jahveh our Righteousness.</hi> Jer 23:7. <hi type="italic">Therefore, behold, days come, saith Jahveh, that they shall no more say: By the life of Jahveh who brought up the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt,</hi> Jer 23:8. <hi type="italic">But: By the life of Jahveh who brought up and led forth the seed of the house of Israel out of the land towards midnight, and out of all the lands whither I had driven them, and they shall dwell in their own land."</hi> <div eID="gen14106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14107" type="x-p"/> This portion is the conclusion of the prophecy concerning the shepherds of Israel, Jer 22. In <reference osisRef="Jer.23.1">Jer 23:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.23.2">Jer 23:2</reference> what has been foretold concerning the last kings of Judah is condensed into one general sentence, so as thus to form a point of connection for the declaration of salvation which follows at <reference osisRef="Jer.23.3">Jer 23:3</reference>, consisting in the gathering again of the people, neglected and scattered by the evil shepherds, by means of the righteous branch of David. The Lord cries woe upon the shepherds. רעים without article, because the matter concerns all evil shepherds, and is not applied till <reference osisRef="Jer.23.2">Jer 23:2</reference> to the evil rulers of Judah. Venema rightly says: <hi type="italic">Generale vae pastoribus malis praemittitur, quod mox ad pastores Judae applicatur</hi>. It is so clear from the context as to have been generally admitted by recent comm., that by shepherds are meant not merely the false prophets and priests, nor even these along with the kings; cf. on <reference osisRef="Jer.3.15">Jer 3:15</reference>; Jer 25:34., and Ezek 34. The flock of my pasturing, in other words, the flock, which I feed; for מרעית sig. both the feeding (cf. Hos 13:6) and the place where the flock feeds, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.25.36">Jer 25:36</reference>; Psa 74:1. Israel is called the flock of Jahveh’s pasturing inasmuch as He exerts a special care over it. The flock bad shepherds, the ungodly monarchs on the throne of David, have brought to ruin and scattered. The scattering is in <reference osisRef="Jer.23.2">Jer 23:2</reference>, cf. with <reference osisRef="Jer.23.3">Jer 23:3</reference>, called a driving out into the lands; but the "destroying" must be discovered from the train of thought, for the clause: ye have not visited them (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.2">Jer 23:2</reference>), intimates merely their neglect of the sheep committed to their charge. What the "destroying" more especially is, we may gather from the conduct of King Jehoiakim, described in Jer 22:13.; it consists in oppression, violence, and the shedding of innocent blood; cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.2">Eze 34:2</reference>-3. With לכן, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.2">Jer 23:2</reference>, is made the application of the general sentence, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.1">Jer 23:1</reference>, to the shepherds of Israel. Because they are such as have scattered, driven away, and not visited the flock of the Lord, therefore He will punish in them the wickedness of their doings. In the לא פקדתּם אתם is summed up all that the rulers have omitted to do for the flock committed to their care; cf. the specification of what they have not done, Eze 34:4. It was their duty, as Ven. truly says, to see <hi type="italic">ut vera religio, pabulum populi spiritualé, recte et rite exerceretur</hi>. Instead of this, they have, by introducing idolatry, directly encouraged ungodliness, and the immorality which flows therefrom. Here in "ye have not visited them" we have the negative moment made prominent, so that in <reference osisRef="Jer.23.3">Jer 23:3</reference> may follow what the Lord will do for His scattered flock. Cf. the further expansion of this promise in Eze 34:12. We must note "I have driven them," since in <reference osisRef="Jer.23.2">Jer 23:2</reference> it was said that the bad shepherds had driven the flock away. The one does not exclude the other. By their corrupting the people, the wicked shepherds had occasioned the driving out; and this God has inflicted on the people as punishment. But the people, too, had their share in the guilt; but to this attention is not here directed, since the question deals only with the shepherds.
entries.29c4c7126cc06ae45cc9034049d154832484922d: <reference osisRef="Jer.23.4-Jer.23.5">Jer 23:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen14107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14108" type="x-p"/> When the Lord shall gather His people out of the dispersion, then will He raise up shepherds over them who will so feed them that they shall no longer need to fear or to be dismayed before enemies who might be strong enough to subjugate, slay, and carry them captive. The figurative expressions are founded on the idea that the sheep, when they are neglected by the shepherds, are torn and devoured by wild beasts; cf. Eze 34:8. They shall not be lacking; cf. for נפקד with this force, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.7">1Sa 25:7</reference>; in substance = not be lost. לא יפּקדוּ is chosen with a view to לא פקדתּם אתם (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.2">Jer 23:2</reference>): because the shepherds did not take charge of the sheep, therefore the sheep are scattered and lost. Hereafter this shall happen no more. The question as to how this promise is to be accomplished is answered by <reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jer 23:5</reference> and Jer 23:6. The substance of these verses is indeed introduced by the phrase: behold, days come, as something new and important, but not as something not to happen till after the things foretold in Jer 23:4. According to Jeremiah’s usage throughout, that phrase does not indicate any progress in time as compared with what precedes, but draws attention to the weightiness of what is to be announced. There is also a suggestion of "the contrast between the hope and the existing condition of affairs, which does not itself justify that hope. However gloomy the present is, yet there is a time coming" (Hgstb.). The promise: I make to arise (raise up) to David a righteous branch, rests upon the promise, <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.12">2Sa 7:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.17.12">1Ch 17:12</reference> : I raise up thy seed after thee, which shall be of thy sons-which the Lord will hereafter fulfil to David. Graf tries to show by many, but not tenable arguments, that צמח has here a collective force. That he is wrong, we may see from the passages Zec 3:8 and Zec 6:12, where the same "branch" foretold by Jeremiah is called the man whose name is צמח; and even without this we may discover the same from the context of the present passage, both from "He shall reign as king," and still more from: they shall call his name <hi type="italic">Jahveh Tsidkenu</hi>. Neither of these sayings can be spoken of a series of kings. Besides, we have the passages <reference osisRef="Jer.30.9">Jer 30:9</reference> and Eze 34:23., <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.24">Eze 37:24</reference>, where the servant to be raised up to David by Jahveh is called "my servant David." Although then צמח has a collective force when it means a plant of the field, it by no means follows that "it has always a collective force" in its transferred spiritual signification. And the passage, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.17">Jer 33:17</reference>, where the promise is explained by: David shall never want a man to sit upon the throne of Israel (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.33.21">Jer 33:21</reference>), does not prove that the branch of David is a collective grouping together of all David’s future posterity, but only that this one branch of David shall possess the throne for ever, and not, like mortal men, for a series of years only; 2Sa 7:16. צמח denotes the Messiah, and this title is formed from צמח, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">Isa 4:2</reference> (see Del. on this passage). Nor does the mention of shepherds in the plural, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.4">Jer 23:4</reference>, at all oppose this. An untenable rendering of the sense is: first I will raise up unto you shepherds, then the Messiah; or: better shepherds, <hi type="italic">inprimis unum, Messiam</hi> (Chr. B. Mich.). The two promises are not so to be joined. First we have the raising up of good shepherds, in contrast to the evil shepherds that have destroyed the people; then the promise is further explained to the effect that these good shepherds shall be raised up to David in the "righteous branch," i.e., in the promised "seed" of his sons. The good shepherds are contrasted with the evil shepherds, but are then summed up in the person of the Messiah, as being comprised therein. The relation of the good shepherds to the righteous branch is not so, that the latter is the most pre-eminent of the former, but that in that one branch of David the people should have given to them all the good shepherds needed for their deliverance. The Messiah does not correspond to the series of David’s earthly posterity that sit upon his throne, in that He too, as second David, will also have a long series of descendants upon His throne; but in that His kingdom, His dominion, lasts for ever. In the parallel passage, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.15">Jer 33:15</reference>, where the contrast to the evil shepherds is omitted, we therefore hear only of the one branch of David; so in Ezek 34, where only the <hi type="italic">one</hi> good shepherd, the servant of the Lord, David, stands in contrast to the evil shepherds (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.23">Jer 23:23</reference>). Hence neither must we seek the fulfilment of our prophecy in the elevation of the Maccabees, who were not even of the race of David, nor understand, as Grot., Zerubbabel to be the righteous branch, but the Messiah, as was rightly understood by the <hi type="italic">Chald</hi>. He is צדּיק in contrast to the then reigning members of the house of David, and as He who will do right and justice in His realm; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.22.15">Jer 22:15</reference>, where the same is said of Josiah as contrasted with his ungodly son Jehoiakim. מלך is subjoined to מלך to bespeak His rule as kingship in the fullest sense of the word. <hi type="italic">Regnabit rex</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">magnifice regnabit, ut non tantum appareant aliquae reliquiae pristinae dignitatis, sed ut rex floreat et vigeat et obtineat perfectionem, qualis fuit sub Davide et Salomone ac multo praestantior</hi> (Calv.). השׂכּיל, deal prudently, rule wisely, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.3.15">Jer 3:15</reference>, not: be fortunate, prosperous. Here the context demands the former rendering, the only one justified by usage, since the doing of right and justice is mentioned as the fruit and result of the השׂכיל. These words, too, point back to David, of whom it is in <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.15">2Sa 8:15</reference> said, that he as king did right and justice to all his people.
entries.311f66bf5037a0c2b9841c4434bb3bf6db0ae382: <reference osisRef="Jer.23.6-Jer.23.8">Jer 23:6-8</reference> <div eID="gen14108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14109" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jer 23:6</reference> exhibits the welfare which the "branch" will, by His wise and just rule, secure for the people. Judah shall be blessed with welfare (נושׁע), and Israel dwell safely; that blessing will come into fulfilment which Moses set before the people’s view in Deu 33:28. יהוּדה as the totality of the inhabitants is construed as feminine, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.3.7">Jer 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.2">Jer 14:2</reference>, etc. <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> denotes the ten tribes. Under the just sceptre of the Messiah, all Israel will reach the destiny designed for it by the Lord, will, as God’s people, attain to full dignity and glory. <div eID="gen14109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14110" type="x-p"/> This is the name by which they shall call Him, the branch of David: Jahveh our Righteousness. The suffix in יקראו refers to "righteous branch." Instead of the 3 <hi type="italic">pers</hi>. <hi type="italic">sing</hi>. יקרא with the suffix ו, some <hi type="italic">codd</hi>. have the plur. יקראוּ. This some polemical authors, such as Raim., Martini, Galatin, hold to be the true reading; and they affirmed the other had proceeded from the Jews, with the design of explaining away the deity of the Messiah. The Jews translated, they said: This is the name whereby Jahveh will call him: Our Righteousness; which is indeed the rendering of R. Saad. Gaon <hi type="italic">apud</hi> Aben Ezra, and of Menasse ben Israel. But this rendering is rejected by most Jewish comm. as being at variance with the accents, so that the impugned reading could not well have been invented by the Jews for polemical purposes. יקראו is attested by most <hi type="italic">codd</hi>., and is rendered by the lxx, so that the sense can be none other than: they will call the righteous branch of David "Jahveh our Righteousness." Most comm., including even Hitz., admit that the suffix refers to צמח, the principal person in both verses. Only Ew., Graf, and Näg. seek to refer it to Israel, because in <reference osisRef="Jer.33.16">Jer 33:16</reference> the same name is given to Jerusalem. But the passage cited does not prove the case. To call any one by a name universally denotes in the prophetic usage: to set him forth as that which the name expresses; so here: the branch of David will manifest Himself to the people of Israel as Jahve Tsidkenu. This name is variously expounded. The older Christian comm. understand that the Messiah is here called Jehovah, and must therefore be true God, and that He is called our righteousness, inasmuch as He justifies us by His merit.<note placement="foot">Thus the <hi type="italic">Vulg</hi>. renders: <hi type="italic">Dominus justus noster</hi>; and even Calv. says: <hi type="italic">Quicunque sine contentione et amarulentia judicant, facile vident, idem nomen competer in Christum, quatenus est Deus, sicuti nomen filii Davidis respectu humanae naturae ei tribuitur. - Omnibus aequis et moderatis hoc constabit, Christum hic insigniri duplici elogio, ut in eo nobis commendet propheta tam deitatis gloriam, quam veritatem humanae naturae</hi>; and by the righteousness he understands justification by the merits of Christ.</note> <div eID="gen14110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14111" type="x-p"/> But the rabbinical interpreters, headed by the Chald., take the name to be an abbreviation of a sentence; so e.g., Kimchi: <hi type="italic">Israel vocabit Messiam hoc nomine, quia ejus temporibus Domini justitia nobis firma, jugis et non recedet</hi>. They appeal to <reference osisRef="Jer.33.17">Jer 33:17</reference> and to other passages, such as <reference osisRef="Exod.17.15">Exo 17:15</reference>, where Moses calls the altar "Jahveh my Banner," and <reference osisRef="Gen.33.20">Gen 33:20</reference>, where Jacob gives to the altar built by him the name <hi type="italic">El elohe Jisrael</hi>. Hgstb. has rightly pronounced for this interpretation. The passages cited show who in such names an entire sentence is conveyed. "Jahveh my Banner" is as much as to say: This altar is dedicated to Jahveh my banner, or to the Almighty, the God of Israel. So all names compounded of <hi type="italic">Jahveh</hi>; e.g., <hi type="italic">Jehoshua</hi> = Jahveh salvation, brief for: he to whom Jahveh vouchsafes salvation. So <hi type="italic">Tsidkijahu</hi> = Jahve’s righteousness, for: he to whom Jahveh deals righteousness. To this corresponds <hi type="italic">Jahveh Tsidkenu</hi>: he by whom Jahveh deals righteousness. We are bound to take the name thus by the parallel passage, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.16">Jer 33:16</reference>, where the same name is given to Jerusalem, to convey the thought, that by the Messiah the Lord will make Jerusalem the city of Righteousness, will give His righteousness to it, will adorn and glorify it therewith. צדקנוּ is not to be referred, as it is by the ancient Church comm., to justification through the forgiveness of sins. With this we have not here to do, but with personal righteousness, which consists in deliverance from all unrighteousness, and which is bound up with blessedness. Actual righteousness has indeed the forgiveness of sins for its foundation, and in this respect justification is not to be wholly excluded; but this latter is here subordinate to actual righteousness, which the Messiah secures for Israel by the righteousness of His reign. The unrighteousness of the former kings has brought Israel and Judah to corruption and ruin; the righteousness of the branch to be hereafter raised up to David will remove all the ruin and mischief from Judah, and procure for them the righteousness and blessedness which is of God. - "What Jeremiah," as is well remarked by Hgstb., "sums up in the name Jehovah Tsidkenu, Ezekiel expands at length in the parallel <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.25-Ezek.34.31">Eze 34:25-31</reference> : the Lord concludes with them a covenant of peace; rich blessings fall to their lot; He breaks their yoke, frees them from bondage; they do not become the heathen’s prey." These divine blessings are also to be conferred upon the people by means of the righteous branch. What the ancient Church comm. found in the <hi type="italic">name</hi> was true as to the <hi type="italic">substance</hi>. For as no man is perfectly righteous, so no mere earthly king can impart to the people the righteousness of Jahveh in the full sense of the term; only He who is endowed with the righteousness of God. In so far the Godhead of this King is contained <hi type="italic">implicite</hi> in the name; only we must not understand that he that bore the name is called Jahveh. But that righteousness, as the sum of all blessing, is set before the people’s view, we may gather from the context, especially from <reference osisRef="Jer.23.7">Jer 23:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.23.8">Jer 23:8</reference>, where it is said that the blessings to be conferred will outshine all former manifestations of God’s grace. This is the sense of both verses, which, save in the matter of a trifling change in <reference osisRef="Jer.23.8">Jer 23:8</reference>, are verbally repeated from <reference osisRef="Jer.16.14">Jer 16:14</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.16.15">Jer 16:15</reference>, where they have already been expounded.<note placement="foot">The lxx have omitted both these verses here, and have placed them at the end of the chapter, after <reference osisRef="Jer.23.40">Jer 23:40</reference>; but by their contents they do not at all belong to that, whereas after <reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jer 23:6</reference> they are very much in place, as even Hitz. admits. In the text of the lxx handed down, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jer 23:6</reference> ends with the words:  ̓Ιωσεδὲκ ἐν τοῖς προφήταις; and  ̓Ιωσεδὲκ  may be said to correspond to יהוה צדקנוּ, and ἐν τοῖς προφήταις  to לנּביאים, Jer 23:9. Hitz. and Gr. therefore infer that <reference osisRef="Jer.23.7">Jer 23:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.23.8">Jer 23:8</reference> were wanting also in the Heb. text used by the translator, and that they must have been added by way of supplement, most probably from another MS. This inference is thought to find support in the assumption that, because the Greek MSS have no point between  ̓Ιωσεδὲκ and ἐν τοῦς προφήταις, therefore the Alexandrian translator must have joined these words together so as to make one - meaningless - sentence. A thoroughly uncritical conclusion, which could be defended only if the Alex. translators had punctuated their Greek text as we have it punctuated in our printed editions. And if a later reader of the lxx had added the verses from the Hebrew text, then he would certainly have intercalated them at the spot where they stood in the original, i.e., between <reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jer 23:6</reference> and Jer 23:9. Their displacement to a position after <reference osisRef="Jer.23.40">Jer 23:40</reference> is to be explained from the fact that in <reference osisRef="Jer.16.14">Jer 16:14</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.16.15">Jer 16:15</reference> they immediately follow a threatening: and is manifestly the work of the translator himself, who omitted them after <reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jer 23:6</reference>, understanding them as of threatening import, because a threatening seemed to him to be out of place after Jer 23:6.</note> <div eID="gen14111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14112" type="x-p"/> Against the False Prophets. - Next to the kings, the pseudo-prophets, who flattered the people’s carnal longings, have done most to contribute to the fall of the realm. Therefore Jeremiah passes directly from his discourse against the wicked kings to rebuking the false prophets; and if we may presume from the main substance, the latter discourse belongs to the same time as the former. It begins
entries.570b2c4eefb6368ecc64daf155f72f5354143470: <reference osisRef="Jer.23.9-Jer.23.11">Jer 23:9-11</reference> <hi type="italic">With a description of the pernicious practices of these persons. -</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.23.9">Jer 23:9</reference> <hi type="italic">. "Concerning the prophets. Broken is mine heart within me; all my bones totter. I am become like a drunken man, and like a man whom wine hath overcome, because of Jahveh and because of His holy words.</hi> Jer 23:10. <hi type="italic">For of adulterers the land is full, for because of the curse the land withereth, the pastures of the wilderness dry up; and their course is become evil, and their strength not right.</hi> Jer 23:11. <hi type="italic">For both prophet and priest are profane; yea, in mine house found I their wickedness, saith Jahveh.</hi> Jer 23:12. <hi type="italic">Therefore their way shall be to them as slippery places in darkness, they shall be thrown down and fall therein; for I bring evil upon them, the year of their visitation, saith Jahveh.</hi> Jer 23:13. <hi type="italic">In the prophets of Samaria saw I folly; they prophesied in the name of Baal, and led my people Israel astray.</hi> Jer 23:14. <hi type="italic">But in the prophets of Jerusalem saw I an horrible thing, committing adultery and walking in falsehood, and they strengthen the hands of the wicked, that none returneth from his wickedness. They are all become to me as Sodom, and the inhabitants thereof as Gomorrah.</hi> Jer 23:15. <hi type="italic">Therefore thus saith Jahveh of hosts concerning the prophets: Behold, I feed them with wormwood, and give them to drink water of bitterness; for from the prophets of Jerusalem is profaneness gone forth over all the land."</hi> "Concerning the prophets" is the heading, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jer 46:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.1">Jer 48:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.1">Jer 49:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.7">Jer 49:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.23">Jer 49:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.28">Jer 49:28</reference>; and corresponds to the woe uttered against the wicked shepherds, Jer 23:1. It refers to the entire portion vv. 9-40, which is thus distinguished from the oracles concerning the kings, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1-Jer.21.14">Jer 21:1-14</reference> and 22. It might indeed be joined, according to the accents, with what follows: because of the prophets is my heart broken; but as the cause of Jeremiah’s deep agitation is given at the end of the second half-verse: because of Jahveh, etc., it is not likely the seer would in one sentence have given two different and quite separate reasons. The brokenness of his heart denotes the profoundest inward emotion yet not despondency by reason of sin and misery, like "a broken heart" in <reference osisRef="Ps.34.19">Psa 34:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.51.19">Psa 51:19</reference>, etc., but because of God’s wrath at the impious lives of the pseudo-prophets. This has overcome him, and this he must publish. This wrath had broken his heart and seized on all his bones, so that they nervelessly tremble, and he resembles a drunken man who can no longer stand firm on his feet. He feels himself inwardly quite downcast; he not only feels the horrors of the judgment that is to befall the false prophets and corrupt priests who lead the people astray, but knows well the dreadful sufferings the people too will have to endure. The verb רחף occurs only twice in the Piel besides in the present passage; in <reference osisRef="Gen.1.2">Gen 1:2</reference>, of the Spirit of God that in the beginning of creation brooded over the waters of the earth, and <reference osisRef="Deut.32.11">Deu 32:11</reference>, of the eagle that flutters over her young - in Arabic <hi type="italic">rchf</hi>, to be soft. The root meaning of the word is doubtless: to be flaccid; here accordingly, to totter, to sway to and fro. "Because of Jahveh" is more fully explained by "because of the words of His holiness," i.e., the words which God as holy has made known to him regarding the unholy ongoings of the pseudo-prophets. - From <reference osisRef="Jer.23.10">Jer 23:10</reference> onwards come the sayings of God which have so terribly agitated the prophet. The land is full of adulterers. Adultery in the literal sense is mentioned by way of example, as a reckless transgression of God’s commands, then much in vogue, whereby the moral foundations of the kingdom were broken up. In <reference osisRef="Jer.23.14">Jer 23:14</reference> the prophets are said to commit adultery and walk in lying, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.29.23">Jer 29:23</reference> and Jer 5:7. By reason of this vice a curse lies on the land, under which it is withering away. The clause "for because of the curse," etc., is not to be taken as parenthesis (Näg.), but as co-ordinate with the previous clause, giving the second, or rather the chief ground, why Jeremiah is so deeply distressed. The reason of this is not so much the prevailing moral corruption, as the curse lying on the land because of the moral corruption of its inhabitants. אלה is not perjury (Chald., Rashi, Kimchi), but the curse wherewith God punishes the transgression of His covenant laws, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.11.3">Jer 11:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.8">Jer 11:8</reference>, Deu 28:15., Jer 29:19. The words are modelled after Isa 24:4.; and הארץ is not the population, but the land itself, which suffers under God’s curse, and which is visited with drought; cf. Jer 12:4. The next words point to drought. נאות מדבּר as in Jer 9:9. By ותּהי the further description of the people’s depravity is attached to the first clause of the verse. Their course is become evil; their running or racing, i.e., the aim and endeavour of the ungodly. The suffix on this word מרוּצתם refers not to "adulterers," but <hi type="italic">ad sensum</hi> to the inhabitants of the land. Their strength is not-right, i.e., they are strong, valiant in wrong; cf. Jer 9:2. For - so goes <reference osisRef="Jer.23.11">Jer 23:11</reference> - both prophets and priests, who should lead the people in the right way, are profane, and desecrate by their wickedness even the house of God, presumably by idolatry; cf. Jer 32:34. There is no reason for thinking here, as Hitz. does, of adultery practised in the temple.
entries.5af56fd1cc4d19d5048a8e752d607dd577a0c118: <reference osisRef="Jer.23.12">Jer 23:12</reference> <div eID="gen14112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14113" type="x-p"/> For this the Lord will punish them. Their way shall be to them as slippery places in darkness. This threatening is after the manner of <reference osisRef="Ps.35.6">Psa 35:6</reference>, where חשׁך are joined, changed by Jeremiah to the words in the text. The passage cited shows that we may not separate בּאפלה from חלקלקּות, as Ew. does, to join it to the following ידּחוּ. Their way shall resemble slippery places in the dark, when one may readily slip and fall. Besides, they are to be thrust, pushed, so that they must fall on the slippery path (ידּחוּ from דּחח = דּחה, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.5">Psa 35:5</reference>; "therein" to be referred to "their way"). The clause: "for I bring evil," etc., is formed after Jer 11:23.
entries.fb06e8faede796b2dbefa33abbee8285b8d43069: <reference osisRef="Jer.23.13-Jer.23.15">Jer 23:13-15</reference> <div eID="gen14113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14114" type="x-p"/> To display the vileness of the prophets, these are parallelized with the prophets of Samaria. The latter did foolishly (תּפלה, prop. of that which is unsalted, insipid, <reference osisRef="Job.6.6">Job 6:6</reference>, hence irrational, <hi type="italic">insulsum</hi>), since they prophesied, being inspired by Baal the no-god, and by such prophesying led the people into error; cf. 1Ki 18:19. Much more horrible is the conduct of the prophets of Jerusalem, who commit adultery, walk in lying, and strengthen the wicked in their wickedness, not merely by their delusive pretences (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.23.17">Jer 23:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.14">Jer 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.13">Jer 14:13</reference>), but also by their immoral lives, so that no one turns from his wickedness, cf. Eze 13:22. לבלתּי is here and in <reference osisRef="Jer.27.18">Jer 27:18</reference>, as in ex. 20:20, construed, contrary to the usage everywhere else, not with the <hi type="italic">infin</hi>., but with the <hi type="italic">verb. fin</hi>. As the prophets, instead of converting the wicked, only confirmed them in their sins, therefore all the inhabitants of Judah or Jerusalem are become as corrupt as Sodom and Gomorrah. "They all" are not the prophets, but the inhabitants of Judah or Jerusalem; and "the inhabitants thereof" are those of the capital, cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.32.32">Deu 32:32</reference>; Isa 1:10. On the seducers the Lord will therefore inflict punishment, because impiousness has gone forth from them over the whole land. With the punishment threatened in <reference osisRef="Jer.23.15">Jer 23:15</reference>, cf. Jer 9:14.
entries.2c8f16aa1195473ef5816aa6e38c8973e2151489: <reference osisRef="Jer.23.16-Jer.23.20">Jer 23:16-20</reference> <hi type="italic">Warning against the lying prophecies of the prophets. -</hi> Jer 23:16. <hi type="italic">"Thus saith Jahveh of hosts: Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you! They deceive you; a vision of their heart they speak, not out of the mouth of Jahveh.</hi> Jer 23:17. <hi type="italic">They say still unto my despisers: 'Jahveh hath spoken: Peace shall ye have;' and unto every one that walketh in the stubbornness of his heart they say: 'There shall no evil come upon you.'</hi> Jer 23:18. <hi type="italic">For who hath stood in Jahveh’s counsel, that he might have seen and heard His word? who hath marked my word and heard it?</hi> Jer 23:19. <hi type="italic">Behold a tempest from Jahveh, fury goeth forth, and eddying whirlwind shall hurl itself upon the head of the wicked.</hi> Jer 23:20. <hi type="italic">The anger of God shall not turn till He have done and till He have performed the thoughts of His heart. At the end of the days shall ye be well aware of this.</hi> Jer 23:21. <hi type="italic">I have not sent the prophets, yet they ran; I have not spoken to them, yet they prophesied.</hi> Jer 23:22. <hi type="italic">But if they had stood in my counsel, they would publish my words to my people and bring them back from their evil way and from the evil of their doings."</hi> <div eID="gen14114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14115" type="x-p"/> The warning against these prophets is founded in <reference osisRef="Jer.23.16">Jer 23:16</reference> on the fact that they give out the thoughts of their own hearts to be divine revelation, and promise peace and prosperity to all stiff-necked sinners. מהבּלים, lit., they make you vain, i.e., make you to yield yourselves to vain delusion, seduce you to false confidence. This they do by their speaking visions, i.e., revelations of their heart, not what God has spoken, revealed to them. As an illustration of this, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.17">Jer 23:17</reference> tells that they prophesy continued peace or well-being to the despisers of God. The <hi type="italic">infin. abs</hi>. אמור after the <hi type="italic">verb. fin</hi>. intimates the duration or repetition of the thing. דּבּר יהוה are words of the false prophets, with which they give out that their prophesyings are God’s word. Since we nowhere else find sayings of Jahveh introduced by דּבּר יהוה, but usually by 'כּה אמר י, the lxx have taken offence at that formula, and, reading דבר, join the words with למנאצי: τοῖς ἀπωθουμένοις τὸν λόγον κυρίου. To this reading Hitz. and Gr. give the preference over the Masoretic; but they have not noticed that they thus get an unsuitable sense. For דבר יהוה in prophetic language never denotes the Mosaic law or the "moral law" (Hitz.), but the word of God published by the prophets. By their view of "word of Jahveh" they would here obtain the self-inconsistent thought: to the despisers of divine revelation they proclaim as revelation. The Masoretic reading is clearly right; and Jeremiah chose the unusual introductory formula to distinguish the language of the pseudo-prophets from that of the true prophets of the Lord. וכל־הלך ב' is prefixed absolutely: and as concerning every one that walks...they say, for: and to every one...they say. On the "stubbornness of their heart," see on Jer 3:17. With the speech of the false prophets, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.14.13">Jer 14:13</reference> and Jer 6:14. - In <reference osisRef="Jer.23.18">Jer 23:18</reference> a more comprehensive reason is given to show that these prophets are not publishing God’s decrees. The question: Who hath stood? has negative force = None hath stood. By this Jeremiah does not deny the possibility of this universally, but only of the false prophets (Hitz.). This limitation of the words is suggested by the context. To the true prophets the Lord reveals His סוד, Amo 3:7. ויראוישׁמע are not to be taken jussively: let him see and hear (Hitz.), for the foregoing interrogation is not a conditional clause introducing a command. The imperfects with ו are clauses of consequence or design, and after a preceding perfect should be rendered in English by the conditional of the pluperfect. Seeing the word of God refers to prophetic vision. The second question is appended without at all conveying any inference from what precedes; and in it the second verb (with ו <hi type="italic">consec</hi>.) is simply a strengthening of the first: who hath hearkened to my word and heard it? The Masoretes have quite unnecessarily changed the <hi type="italic">Chet</hi>. דּברי .tehC  into דּברו. In the graphic representation of the prophets, the transition to the direct speech of God, and conversely, is no unusual thing. The change of ויּשׁמע into ישׁמע, unnecessary and even improper as it is, is preferred by Graf and Näg., inasmuch as they take the interrogative מי in both clauses in the sense of <hi type="italic">quisquis</hi> and understand the verse thus: He who has but stood in the counsel of the Lord, let him see and hear His word (i.e., he must see and hear His word); and he that hath marked my word, let him publish it (i.e., he must publish it). This exposition becomes only then necessary, if we leave the context out of view and regard the question as being to the effect that no one has stood in God’s counsel - which Jeremiah could not mean. Not to speak of the change of the text necessary for carrying it through, this view does not even give a suitable sense. If the clause: He that has stood in the counsel of the Lord, he must proclaim His word, is to be regarded as having a demonstrative force, then the principal idea must be supplied, thus namely: "and it is impossible that it should be favourable to those who despise it." In <reference osisRef="Jer.23.19">Jer 23:19</reference> Jeremiah publishes a real word of the Lord, which sounds very differently from the words of the false prophets. A tempest from Jahveh will burst over the heads of the evil-doers, and the wrath of God will not cease until it has accomplished the divine decree. "A tempest from Jahveh" is defined by "fury" in apposition as being a manifestation of God’s wrath; and the whole first clause is further expanded in the second part of the verse. The tempest from Jahveh goes forth, i.e., breaks out, and as whirling tornado or eddying whirlwind bursts over the head of the wicked. יחוּל is to be taken in accordance with מתחולל: twist, whirl, cf. 2Sa 3:29. "The thoughts of His heart" must not be limited to what God has decreed <hi type="italic">de interitu populi</hi> (Calv.); it comprehends God’s whole redemptive plan in His people’s regard-not merely the overthrow of the kingdom of Judah, but also the purification of the people by means of judgments and the final glorification of His kingdom. To this future the next clause points: at the end of the days ye shall have clear knowledge of this. "The end of the days" is not merely the completion of the period in which we now are (Hitz., Gr. Näg., etc.), but, as universally, the end of the times, i.e., the Messianic future, the last period of the world’s history which opens at the close of the present aeon; see on <reference osisRef="Gen.49.1">Gen 49:1</reference>; Num 24:14, etc. התבּונן is strengthened by בּינה yb dene: attain to insight, come to clearer knowledge.
entries.ad608e5d88f168e9683b28da89b05e29e7f5a020: <reference osisRef="Jer.23.21-Jer.23.22">Jer 23:21-22</reference> <div eID="gen14115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14116" type="x-p"/> From the word of the Lord proclaimed in Jer 23:19. it appears that the prophets who prophesy peace or well-being to the despisers of God are not sent and inspired by God. If they had stood in the counsel of God, and so had truly learnt God’s word, they must have published it and turned the people from its evil way. This completely proves the statement of <reference osisRef="Jer.23.16">Jer 23:16</reference>, that the preachers of peace deceive the people. Then follows -
